title: Research frontier status and calibrated model evidence

items.title: Research status for the Navier–Stokes regularity frontier
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement:
Use the whole-space, incompressible constant-density Navier–Stokes equations in Euclidean coordinates as the formulation under discussion:

$$\partial_t u+(u\cdot\nabla)u-\nu\Delta u+\nabla p=f,\qquad \nabla\cdot u=0.$$

Here $u:\mathbb R^3\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^3$ is velocity in metres per second. Let $\rho_0>0$ be the constant mass density in kilograms per cubic metre. The scalar fields $P,p:\mathbb R^3\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ are the mechanical pressure $P$ in pascals and the reduced pressure $p:=P/\rho_0$ in square metres per square second. The vector field $f:\mathbb R^3\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^3$ is force per unit mass in metres per square second. Fix a constant kinematic viscosity $\nu>0$ in square metres per second. In the global smooth solution assertions below, $u,P,p$ are $C^\infty$ on this space-time domain; the admissible forcing $f$ is also $C^\infty$ there. Set reference scales $\ell_0:=1\,\mathrm m$ and $\tau_0:=1\,\mathrm s$ for the dimensionless decay weights below. The gradient and Laplacian act in $x$, with $(u\cdot\nabla)u_i:=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $\Delta u_i:=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2u_i$, and $\nabla\cdot u:=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$; incompressible means $\nabla\cdot u=0$. Smooth means that all space-time partial derivatives of all orders exist and are continuous for $t>0$ and extend continuously to $t=0$, with time derivatives there interpreted from the right. Define the kinetic-energy functional normalized by the constant density as $E(t):=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u(x,t)|^2\,dx$, with SI units $\mathrm{m^5\,s^{-2}}$, and the mechanical kinetic energy as $K(t):=\rho_0E(t)$, in joules. Fefferman's bounded-energy condition is $\sup_{t\ge0}E(t)<\infty$, equivalently $\sup_{t\ge0}K(t)<\infty$ for this fixed positive $\rho_0$. The equation is a mathematical model; no measured flow or physical singularity is asserted. The period-one comparison domain is $\mathbb T^3:=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$ in nondimensional coordinates $X=x/\ell_0$; in SI spatial coordinates, period one means $g(x+\ell_0e_j,t)=g(x,t)$ for each standard coordinate vector $e_j$ and every $t$.

Fefferman’s alternatives are four distinct assertions. Alternative A is the whole-space unforced assertion: for every smooth divergence-free initial field $u^0$ satisfying the stated whole-space decay bound, there exists a global smooth pair $p,u$ solving the displayed equation with $f=0$, $\nabla\cdot u=0$, and $u(x,0)=u^0(x)$, with $\sup_{t\ge0}E(t)<\infty$. Alternative B is the periodic unforced assertion: for every smooth divergence-free period-one initial field $u^0$, there exists a global smooth pair $p,u$ solving the equation with $f=0$, $\nabla\cdot u=0$, and $u(x,0)=u^0(x)$, with $u$ period one in each spatial coordinate; $p$ is required to be smooth but need not be period one. Alternative B imposes no separate uniform-in-time energy bound. Alternative C asks for a smooth divergence-free whole-space initial field $u^0$ and a smooth force $f$ satisfying the whole-space decay bounds below for which no global smooth pair satisfying the equation with that $f$, incompressibility, $u(x,0)=u^0(x)$, and $\sup_{t\ge0}E(t)<\infty$ exists. Alternative D asks for smooth divergence-free period-one initial data $u^0$ and a smooth period-one force $f$ satisfying the periodic decay bound below for which no global smooth solution with that force, $u(x,0)=u^0(x)$, and period-one velocity exists; its pressure is required to be smooth but need not be period one. The energy bound is part of alternatives A and C; in B and D the velocity must be smooth and period one and the pressure smooth, with no separate uniform-in-time energy condition or pressure-periodicity condition.

On $\mathbb R^3$, admissible initial data $u^0$ and force $f$ satisfy, for every multi-index $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)\in\mathbb N_0^3$ and integer $K\ge0$, $|\partial_x^\alpha u^0(x)|\le C_{\alpha K}(1+|x|/\ell_0)^{-K}$, where $\partial_x^\alpha:=\partial_{x_1}^{\alpha_1}\partial_{x_2}^{\alpha_2}\partial_{x_3}^{\alpha_3}$, and, for every $\alpha$ and nonnegative integers $m,K$, $|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_t^m f(x,t)|\le C_{\alpha mK}(1+|x|/\ell_0+t/\tau_0)^{-K}$. Here $|x|$ is the Euclidean norm, and the finite constants have the units required by their respective bounds. On $\mathbb T^3$, the initial field and force are period one in each nondimensional spatial coordinate and, for every $\alpha$ and nonnegative integers $m,K$, $|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_t^m f(x,t)|\le C_{\alpha mK}(1+t/\tau_0)^{-K}$. For specified whole-space data $u^0,f$, a global bounded-energy solution is a pair $p,u\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times[0,\infty))$ satisfying the displayed equation, incompressibility, and $u(x,0)=u^0(x)$, with $\sup_{t\ge0}E(t)<\infty$. For specified periodic data $u^0,f$, a global smooth solution with periodic velocity is a pair $p,u\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times[0,\infty))$ satisfying the same equation, incompressibility, and $u(x,0)=u^0(x)$, with $u$ period one in each spatial coordinate; no periodicity condition is imposed on $p$.

As checked on 2026-10-23 Australia/Sydney, the current Clay problem page labels the entry “Active”. Its announcement of 11 September 2026 says the problem has “apparently” been settled and that evaluation and credit assignment are deliberately unhurried. OpenAI’s announcement and preprint claim to establish alternative C by constructing, for each $\nu>0$, a force $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times(0,\infty);\mathbb R^3)$ and smooth fields $u,p$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[0,1)$ with $u(\cdot,0)=0$, $\nabla\cdot u=0$, $\operatorname{supp}u(\cdot,t)\cup\operatorname{supp}p(\cdot,t)\subset\mathcal K$ for a compact $\mathcal K\subset\mathbb R^3$, $\sup_{0\le t<1}\|u(t)\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}<\infty$, and $\limsup_{t\uparrow1}\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^3)}=\infty$. Here $C_c^\infty$ denotes smooth fields vanishing outside a compact subset of space-time, support is the closure of the set where a field is nonzero, $\|u(t)\|_{L^2}^2=\int|u(x,t)|^2\,dx$, and $\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty}$ is the essential supremum of $|u(x,t)|$ over $x$. The preprint also states that this construction yields alternative D on $\mathbb T^3$ and that no global smooth solution with the same force and initial data can have uniformly bounded energy. This reported forced construction does not establish either zero-force alternative A or B.

An arXiv paper posted on 6 October 2026 reports discrepancies between the preprint and its accompanying Lean formalization: among its examples, the stated inverse estimate in equation (8.19) uses $m+4$ input derivatives while a cited Lean estimate uses $m+5$, and the formalized pressure-flux estimate corresponding to equation (10.19) has a different bound. The authors explicitly do not decide whether the natural-language proof is correct. This item therefore records a dated announced claim and a reported formalization concern; it neither accepts nor refutes the claimed theorem, and does not treat it as an established proof supplier.
items.physical_scope: Dated status reporting for the mathematical regularity problem of the three-dimensional incompressible constant-density Navier–Stokes model; it makes no empirical claim about real-fluid singularities and supplies no accepted proof.

items.title: Evidence scope for calibrated and learned fluid models
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement:
For this remark, a computational fluid-dynamics model is the specified fluid equations together with a numerical algorithm and its code, mapping initial data, boundary data, parameters, and time to calculated fields or quantities of interest. A context of use is the stated set of geometries, initial and boundary conditions, parameter ranges, time interval, output quantities, and required accuracy for which a prediction is intended. A benchmark is a finite set of specified input cases, reference outputs, target quantities, comparison metric, and scoring procedure. Calibration is the selection of adjustable model parameters to fit identified data; training is the corresponding parameter-fitting process for a learned component. A held-out evaluation set is not used to fit those parameters, although it may still be generated by the same numerical reference model.

Code verification checks that the code implements the stated mathematical model; solution verification estimates numerical error for a particular calculation. Physical-model validation assesses agreement with relevant observations of the physical system for the stated context of use, with experimental and computational uncertainty accounted for. These are different claims: a numerical verification benchmark does not establish physical realism, and an algorithmic held-out score is not, by itself, physical-model validation.

Accordingly, a calibrated or learned model’s reported score supports only the specified cases, reference outputs, quantities, metric, and evaluation protocol. If the reference outputs are themselves computed by a fluid solver, agreement with them is evidence about the learned component relative to that solver and its assumptions, not direct evidence about an actual fluid. Extrapolation to other geometries, boundary conditions, forcing, parameter ranges, time horizons, or measured flows is a separate claim that requires its own evidence. Reports should identify the intended use, training and evaluation data, reference source, comparison metric, baselines, and relevant numerical, input, and measurement uncertainties; a fit to calibration data alone does not establish accuracy for other uses.
items.physical_scope: Methodological scope of computational and learned fluid models for specified input cases and intended uses; no performance claim is made for an unnamed model or unreported physical measurement.

items.title: A four-axis parameterized family of planar velocity fields
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement: Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a nonempty open planar spatial region with coordinates $x,y$ in metres, let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval measured in seconds, and let $\Theta\subset(0,\infty)$ be a nonempty open interval of dimensionless Reynolds numbers. Fix a characteristic speed $U>0$ in metres per second and characteristic length $L>0$ in metres. For each $\theta\in\Theta$, set the kinematic viscosity to $\nu(\theta):=UL/\theta$ in square metres per second, so that the Reynolds number $UL/\nu(\theta)$ equals $\theta$. A parameterized velocity family is a continuously differentiable map $u:\Omega\times I\times\Theta\to\mathbb R^2$ whose value is a planar velocity vector in metres per second; no equation or computed value is stipulated. Sampling this family on grids in $x,y,t,\theta$ gives a data array with four independent input axes. For fixed $\theta$, its spatial domain remains $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ and its physical space-time coordinates are $x,y,t$: Reynolds number indexes different simulation settings and is not an additional spatial or time coordinate, and the two output components of $u$ are not input axes.
items.physical_scope: A constructed nonrelativistic Euclidean data-domain example for a family of planar velocity fields; it asserts no numerical result, experiment, or physical prediction.
